fetched_contents.text: Piroxicam (Feldene): Uses, Side Effects, Interactions, Pictures, Warnings & Dosing What is piroxicam used for? Piroxicam is commonly used to treat the pain and inflammation caused by rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis. Piroxicam may also be used for other conditions as determined by your healthcare provider. How does piroxicam work (mechanism of action)? Piroxicam works by blocking certain substances in the body that cause pain, inflammation, and fever. How is piroxicam supplied (dosage forms)? Piroxicam is available as Feldene and generic piroxicam in the following dosage forms that are taken by mouth. * 10 mg oral tablets * 20 mg oral tablets How should I store piroxicam? Piroxicam should be stored at room temperature, between 68 F to 77 F (20 C to 25 C). It can be exposed to temperatures between 59 F to 86 F (15 C to 30 C), for shorter periods of time, such as when transporting it. Store in a cool, dry place. Side Effects What are the most common side effects of piroxicam? The most common side effects of piroxicam are listed below. Tell your healthcare provider if you have any of these side effects that bother you. * Nausea or vomiting * Constipation or diarrhea * Gas or heartburn * Stomach pain * Headache * Dizziness * Fluid retention (edema) * Rash There may be other side effects of piroxicam that are not listed here. Contact your healthcare provider if you think you are having a side effect of a medicine. In the U.S., you can report side effects to the FDA at www.fda.gov/medwatch or by calling 800-FDA-1088. In Canada, you can report side effects to Health Canada at www.health.gc.ca/medeffect or by calling 866-234-2345. What are the serious side effects of piroxicam? While less common, the most serious side effects of piroxicam are described below, along with what to do if they happen. Heart Attack and Stroke. Piroxicam can increase your risk of a heart attack or stroke that can lead to death. This risk is increased in people with existing heart disease and with longer use of piroxicam and higher doses. Do not take piroxicam if you have had a recent heart attack without talking to your healthcare provider. This could increase your risk of having another heart attack. Get emergency help if you have any of the following symptoms of a heart attack or stroke. * Chest pain or pressure * Fast or abnormal heartbeat * Trouble breathing * Pain in your back, jaw, throat, or arm * Sweating, upset stomach, vomiting, or dizziness * Sudden weakness on one side of your body * Sudden and severe headache * Slurred speech or trouble understanding speech Bleeding. Piroxicam can increase your risk of bleeding, especially if you have a bleeding disorder or take other medicines that increase your risk of bleeding. Tell your healthcare provider right away if you notice signs of bleeding including easy bruising or bleeding. Stomach Bleeding. Piroxicam can increase your risk of bleeding, ulcers, and tears (perforation) in your gut. The risk is higher if you have a history of stomach ulcers, or bleeding problems, take higher doses of piroxicam or take it for longer than directed, have poor health, are age 60 or older, have liver disease, smoke, drink alcohol, or take certain other medicines such as oral corticosteroids, anticoagulants, or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Stop taking piroxicam and get emergency help right away if you have any of the following symptoms. * Vomit blood * Black or tarry poop * Stomach pain that does not go away * Upset stomach * Feel faint Liver Damage. Liver damage, also called hepatotoxicity, can happen when taking piroxicam. Call your healthcare provider right away if you have any of the following symptoms of liver damage. * Nausea or vomiting * Stomach or belly pain * Fever * Weakness or unusual tiredness * Itching * Loss of appetite * Light-colored poop * Dark-colored urine * Your skin or the whites of your eyes turning yellowish in color (also called jaundice) Increased Blood Pressure (Hypertension). Piroxicam may increase your blood pressure or worsen it if you have a history of high blood pressure. Call your healthcare provider if your blood pressure increases while taking this medicine. If you measure your blood pressure and the top number (systolic) is 180 mm Hg or higher or the bottom number (diastolic) is 120 mm Hg or higher, get medical attention right away. An increase in blood pressure may not be noticeable but look out for any of the following symptoms of severely high blood pressure. * Sudden, severe headache * Chest pain * Dizziness or confusion * Trouble breathing * Nausea/vomiting * Blurry or other changes to the vision * Anxiety * Buzzing in the ears * Nosebleed * Feeling of skipped heartbeats Heart Failure. Piroxicam may increase your risk for heart failure. Tell your healthcare provider right away if you have any of the following symptoms of heart failure. * Shortness of breath or trouble breathing, especially while lying down * Swelling in your feet, ankles, or legs (edema) * Unusually fast weight gain * Unusual tiredness Kidney Damage. Kidney damage can happen when taking piroxicam. Stop taking piroxicam and call your healthcare provider right away if you have any of the following symptoms of kidney damage. * Reduced need to pee * Swelling in your feet, ankles, or legs (edema) * Weakness or unusual tiredness * Difficulty catching your breath or chest pain/pressure * Confusion * Nausea * Seizures Increased Potassium Level (Hyperkalemia). Piroxicam can increase the potassium levels in your blood (hyperkalemia), especially if your kidneys are not working as well as they should. Mild increases in potassium may not cause any symptoms. Stop taking the medicine and get help right away if you have any of the following symptoms of sudden, severe high potassium. * Chest pain or fast or abnormal heartbeat * Shortness of breath * Nausea or vomiting * Unable to move your muscles Severe Skin Reactions. Branch 2: Established headache treatments and how they compare

The evidence shows that migraine and headache treatment is organized into acute, preventive, and sometimes nonpharmacologic approaches, with triptans, CGRP inhibitors, and preventive therapies occupying distinct roles.

First-line or commonly used medications for headaches include triptans and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The evidence states that “Common over-the-counter (OTC) migraine medications include acetaminophen (Tylenol), nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and caffeine” [N3-R2], and that acute migraine can be treated with “simple pain relievers and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)” [N3-R5]. Triptans are also described as “common first-choice treatments” for acute migraine [N4-R3], while CGRP antagonists are usually considered when another option is needed [N4-R2]. That distinction matters: triptans target serotonin pathways and are effective for migraine attacks, whereas CGRP inhibitors block the calcitonin gene-related peptide pathway and are generally used for preventive or rescue treatment rather than as first-line acute therapy [N4-R2][N4-R4]. The evidence also notes that anti-CGRP mAbs outperformed BTX-A in reducing monthly headache days at 6 months in a real-world comparison [N4-R4], but that Botox remains a separate preventive option, especially for chronic migraine with neck tension and scheduled visits [N4-R5]. This shows that treatment choice depends on whether the goal is immediate relief, longer-term prevention, or rescue after failure of acute treatment.

Triptans, CGRP inhibitors, and preventive therapies differ primarily in mechanism and indication. Triptans are acute abortive drugs used for migraine attacks, and the evidence says they are “the current gold-standard for acute migraine treatment” [N4-R3]. CGRP inhibitors are described as usually considered when you need another option, and the evidence explicitly compares triptans and CGRP antagonists [N4-R2]. That means CGRP inhibitors are not simply a substitute for triptans; they are an alternative class with a different target and often used when triptans are ineffective or contraindicated [N4-R2][N4-R4]. Preventive therapies are broader and include Botox, anti-CGRP mAbs, and other long-term strategies. The evidence notes that Botox is “cost friendly in a long run” and that anti-CGRP mAbs outperformed BTX-A in some settings [N4-R1][N4-R4], while Botox is still favored for chronic migraine patients with prominent neck tension [N4-R5]. So preventive therapy is not one-size-fits-all: it depends on headache frequency, pattern, comorbidities, and patient preference.

Patient experiences and side-effect profiles matter most because the evidence emphasizes safety, tolerability, and real-world tradeoffs. For triptans, the evidence states that they are “not safe or effective for every person” [N4-R3], which is important because not all patients will tolerate them well. For CGRP inhibitors, the evidence does not provide specific patient experience details in the provided excerpts, but it does support their comparative effectiveness in reducing monthly headache days [N4-R4]. For Botox, the evidence highlights that it excels for patients who prefer scheduled clinic visits and that CGRP monoclonal antibodies offer convenience [N4-R5]. Safety signals from the headache medicine branch are thinner in the current evidence set, but the broader safety branch shows that NSAIDs carry serious cardiovascular and gastrointestinal risks, including myocardial infarction, stroke, bleeding, ulcers, perforation, and kidney injury, and that elderly patients and those with prior GI problems are at greater risk [N5-F3][N5-F4]. The evidence also notes that piroxicam increases the risk of heart attack or stroke, especially with longer use and higher doses, and that it increases bleeding, ulcers, and perforation of the gut [N5-F4].

The practical implication is that patients should not assume all headache treatments are equally suitable. Triptans are acute, CGRP inhibitors are usually considered after triptans, and Botox/anti-CGRP mAbs are preventive. Patient experience matters because some people may prefer scheduled visits, others may want convenience, and others may have contraindications that make one class more or less tolerable. The side-effect profiles matter because the evidence clearly shows that NSAIDs and similar drugs can cause serious cardiovascular and GI harms [N5-F3][N5-F4], while triptans may not be safe for every person [N4-R3]. In short, established headache treatment is a stepwise, evidence-based approach, and the choice depends on headache type, frequency, patient preference, and risk profile.

The evidence strongly supports the conclusion that Miradene is not a separate drug or a new headache-specific medication, but rather a brand name for piroxicam, an NSAID. The Alodokter page explicitly states that “Miradene adalah obat untuk meredakan nyeri dan peradangan” and that “Tiap kapsul Miradene mengandung 10 mg piroxicam” [N1-F2]. It also says Miradene belongs to the NSAID class and is available only with a prescription [N1-F2]. The WebMD page confirms that piroxicam is commonly used for rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis and that it is marketed as Feldene [N1-F1]. The Wikipedia entry describes piroxicam as an NSAID used to relieve symptoms of painful inflammatory conditions like arthritis [N1-R2]. The Mayo Clinic and Drugs.com pages similarly describe piroxicam as an NSAID used for arthritis-related pain and inflammation [N1-R3][N1-R4]. Taken together, these sources make a clear case that Miradene is a brand name for piroxicam, not a distinct drug.

The likely active ingredient is piroxicam, and the indication it is marketed for is pain and inflammation associated with rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and other inflammatory conditions. The evidence states that Miradene is “used to treat the pain and inflammation caused by rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis” [N1-F2], and that piroxicam is used “to treat pain and help relieve symptoms of arthritis (eg, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis)” [N1-R3]. The evidence also notes that piroxicam may be used for other conditions as determined by the healthcare provider [N1-F1], but the Alodokter page is more specific about its use in rheumatic conditions [N1-F2]. The evidence does not support a separate headache-specific indication for Miradene; instead, it supports its use for arthritis and inflammatory pain.

The evidence does not support Miradene as a legitimate headache-specific treatment. The strongest headache-related evidence in the provided sources is about triptans, CGRP inhibitors, and preventive therapies, not Miradene [N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4]. The headache treatment evidence does not mention Miradene or suggest it is used for migraine or acute headache [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5]. The only headache-related mention in the Miradene evidence is that it is a pain-and-inflammation NSAID, not a headache-specific medicine [N1-F2]. That means any claim that Miradene is marketed for headaches is not supported by the evidence and may be mistaken.

The evidence also does not support Miradene as a placeholder, promotional product, or mispronounced name. The Alodokter page is a legitimate Indonesian medical source that identifies Miradene as an NSAID with a prescription requirement and active ingredient piroxicam [N1-F2]. The WebMD and Wikipedia pages confirm the identity of piroxicam/Feldene and describe it as a well-established NSAID [N1-R1][N1-R2]. The Sermo and Drugs.com pages provide safety and physician-rating information for Feldene, reinforcing that it is a real prescription drug with established safety signals and limitations [N5-F3][N5-F4].
